questiontext.text:
Question ID: STAT_U01_L05_Q01

MLA Standard: MLA.STAT.STQ.2

A bar chart title is Favorite Weekend Activity. What does the title identify?

answer.text: The exact value of every data point

feedback.text: A title gives context, not every value.

answer.text: The context of the data display

feedback.text: The title tells what the display is about.
A title does not prove cause.
Scale intervals are found on an axis, not in the title.

questiontext.text:
Question ID: STAT_U01_L05_Q02

MLA Standard: MLA.STAT.STQ.2

A vertical axis says Frequency. What does frequency mean in the display?

feedback.text: Percent is relative frequency, not frequency.
Categories are labels, not counts.
Frequency is a quantity, not the title.
Frequency is the number of cases in a category or interval.

questiontext.text:
Question ID: STAT_U01_L05_Q03

MLA Standard: MLA.STAT.STQ.2

A histogram bar over 20-29 has height 8. What does that mean?

feedback.text: The bar height is frequency, not average.

answer.text: Eight values fall in the interval from 20 to 29

feedback.text: Histogram bar height shows how many values are in that interval.
The interval length is determined by endpoints.
20 is part of the interval label, not the frequency.

questiontext.text:
Question ID: STAT_U01_L05_Q04

MLA Standard: MLA.STAT.STQ.2

In a scatterplot, what do the horizontal and vertical axes usually show?

feedback.text: Category-only variables do not fit a standard scatterplot.
A frequency table is not shown by two scatterplot axes.
Parts of a whole are shown by pie or segmented bar displays.
Scatterplot axes show paired numerical measurements.

questiontext.text:
Question ID: STAT_U01_L05_Q05

MLA Standard: MLA.STAT.STQ.2

A pie chart slice is labeled 25%. What does that quantity represent?

feedback.text: A percent is not a count unless the total is known.

answer.text: One category is one-fourth of the whole

feedback.text: 25% means one part out of the whole group.
Percent is a share, not rank.
A pie chart does not show causation.

questiontext.text:
Question ID: STAT_U01_L05_Q06

MLA Standard: MLA.STAT.STQ.2

Which conclusion is reasonable from a bar chart showing counts by favorite subject?

answer.text: The tallest bar represents the subject with the most responses

feedback.text: In a count bar chart, taller means more responses.

answer.text: The tallest bar caused students to choose the subject

feedback.text: Counts do not prove cause.

answer.text: The average subject is the tallest bar

feedback.text: Category labels cannot be averaged.

answer.text: Every student likes only that subject

feedback.text: Other bars may also have responses.

questiontext.text:
Question ID: STAT_U01_L05_Q07

MLA Standard: MLA.STAT.STQ.2

A display has no units on a numerical axis. What problem can this create?

feedback.text: Missing units do not change the data type.

answer.text: The graph proves no pattern exists

feedback.text: Labels do not determine whether a pattern exists.

answer.text: The quantities may be hard to interpret correctly

feedback.text: Units explain what the numerical values measure.
Assessment choices are unrelated to graph labels.

questiontext.text:
Question ID: STAT_U01_L05_Q08

MLA Standard: MLA.STAT.STQ.2

A relative frequency table gives values 0.20, 0.35, and 0.45. What do these values represent?

feedback.text: Relative frequencies are parts of the total.
The values are numerical proportions.
They are quantities, not labels.
Relative frequencies summarize data; they do not prove causes.

questiontext.text:
Question ID: STAT_U01_L05_Q09

MLA Standard: MLA.STAT.STQ.2

A box plot has a long right whisker. What component is being interpreted?

feedback.text: Box plots summarize numerical data.
That describes pie charts or segmented bars.
That describes scatterplots.

answer.text: Spread on the high-value side of the distribution

feedback.text: A longer whisker shows more spread in that direction.

questiontext.text:
Question ID: STAT_U01_L05_Q10

MLA Standard: MLA.STAT.STQ.2

Which statement avoids overclaiming from a data display?

answer.text: The display proves one variable caused the other

feedback.text: Most displays alone do not prove causation.

answer.text: The display explains every student behavior

feedback.text: Displays summarize data and have limits.

answer.text: The display shows an association in this data set

feedback.text: This describes what is shown without claiming cause.
Labels are needed for interpretation.

questiontext.text:
Question ID: STAT_U01_L05_Q11

MLA Standard: MLA.STAT.STQ.2

A bar chart category has height 12. What additional information is needed to convert that count to a percent?

feedback.text: Color does not determine percent.
Percent equals category count divided by total responses.
Name length is irrelevant.
Font size is formatting, not data.

questiontext.text:
Question ID: STAT_U01_L05_Q12

MLA Standard: MLA.STAT.STQ.2

Which display component tells what each axis measures?

feedback.text: Axis labels identify variables and units.
Color is formatting.
Borders do not identify variables.
Answer letters are not graph components.

questiontext.text:
Question ID: STAT_U01_L05_Q13

MLA Standard: MLA.STAT.STQ.2

A graph shows bus: 30 students and car: 20 students. What quantity is 30?

feedback.text: The number is a count for that category.
A count is not a relative frequency unless divided by total.
Bus is a category, not an interval.
The count does not show cause.

questiontext.text:
Question ID: STAT_U01_L05_Q14

MLA Standard: MLA.STAT.STQ.2

A student says the largest pie slice means that group caused the result. What is the error?

answer.text: A largest slice shows largest share, not cause

feedback.text: Pie charts show proportions, not causation.

answer.text: Pie charts cannot have large slices

feedback.text: Pie slices can vary in size.
Categories can be counted.
Pie charts can show percentages visually.

questiontext.text:
Question ID: STAT_U01_L05_Q15

MLA Standard: MLA.STAT.STQ.2

Which interpretation fits a scatterplot point at (3, 80) for hours studied and test score?

feedback.text: The point is a pair, not a count of students.

answer.text: One student studied 3 hours and scored 80

feedback.text: A point represents paired values for one case.
The coordinates are variable values, not necessarily counts.
The x-value is hours studied, not average score.

questiontext.text:
Question ID: STAT_U01_L05_Q16

MLA Standard: MLA.STAT.STQ.2

What does scale help determine on a graph?

feedback.text: Scale does not prove cause.
Categories can be displayed with or without numerical scale.

answer.text: How numerical distances and quantities are read

feedback.text: Scale controls how values are marked and interpreted.
Standards are separate from graph scale.

questiontext.text:
Question ID: STAT_U01_L05_Q17

MLA Standard: MLA.STAT.STQ.2

Which is the best first step when interpreting a display?

answer.text: Assume the tallest mark proves cause

feedback.text: Height shows quantity, not cause.
Units are essential for accurate interpretation.
Title and labels establish context, variables, and units.
Category names cannot be averaged.

questiontext.text:
Question ID: STAT_U01_L05_Q18

MLA Standard: MLA.STAT.STQ.2

A segmented bar graph compares percentages by grade. What do segment lengths represent?

feedback.text: Segment lengths show proportions for categories within each group.
Segmented bars usually compare proportions.
Median applies to numerical data.
The graph summarizes groups.

questiontext.text:
Question ID: STAT_U01_L05_Q19

MLA Standard: MLA.STAT.STQ.2

Which display component identifies categories in a bar chart?

feedback.text: Intervals belong to histograms.
That measures strength of numerical association.
That belongs to box plots.
Category labels name the groups being compared.

questiontext.text:
Question ID: STAT_U01_L05_Q20

MLA Standard: MLA.STAT.STQ.2

A histogram has bars for intervals, but no title. What is missing?

feedback.text: The bars may still show values by interval.
Histograms use intervals, not category labels.

answer.text: Context for what the data values represent

feedback.text: Without a title, the viewer may not know what is being measured.
Graphs do not include quiz answer letters.

questiontext.text:
Question ID: STAT_U01_L05_Q21

MLA Standard: MLA.STAT.STQ.2

Which statement is supported by a display showing 60% prefer online review?

feedback.text: Preference data alone does not prove grade effects.
Percent is not count unless total is known.
If 60% prefer online, 40% prefer something else or are in other categories.

answer.text: A majority of the group prefers online review

feedback.text: 60% is more than half.

questiontext.text:
Question ID: STAT_U01_L05_Q22

MLA Standard: MLA.STAT.STQ.2

In a histogram, why are the bars usually adjacent?

feedback.text: That describes bar charts, not histograms.
Bar placement does not prove cause.
Histograms show one numerical variable.

answer.text: The intervals represent connected ranges of numerical data

feedback.text: Adjacent bars show continuous or ordered numerical intervals.

questiontext.text:
Question ID: STAT_U01_L05_Q23

MLA Standard: MLA.STAT.STQ.2

What should a supported conclusion include?

answer.text: A claim about causes not shown

feedback.text: Unsupported cause claims overreach.

answer.text: A guess unrelated to the labels

feedback.text: Conclusions should connect to the display.

answer.text: A statement tied to the variables and quantities shown

feedback.text: A good conclusion uses the display evidence and context.

answer.text: A replacement for the data source

feedback.text: A conclusion does not replace the data.

questiontext.text:
Question ID: STAT_U01_L05_Q24

MLA Standard: MLA.STAT.STQ.2

A two-way table shows counts by grade and transportation method. What kind of data is represented?

feedback.text: There are two categorical variables.
Grade and transportation method are categories.
No measured quantities are paired as variables.
The table organizes categorical counts.

questiontext.text:
Question ID: STAT_U01_L05_Q25

MLA Standard: MLA.STAT.STQ.2

Which question checks whether a conclusion is reasonable?

answer.text: Does the display actually show evidence for the claim?

feedback.text: Conclusions must be supported by the displayed data.
Color does not determine statistical support.
The title provides context.

answer.text: Can labels be replaced with guesses?

feedback.text: Labels should not be guessed or ignored.
